decidedBy: the project owner, 2026-09-13, on how the encyclopedia holds Abimelech of Gerar, Phicol and Ahuzzath — recorded as PRB-0497
policy: Abimelech king of Gerar, who deals with Abraham (GEN 20-21) and again with Isaac after Abraham's death (GEN 26), and the Abimelech of the title of Psalm 34, whom 1 Samuel 21 calls Achish king of Gath, are not established as one man. The name is likely a title of the Philistine kings, as Pharaoh is of the kings of Egypt, and at the least it is not certainly one person; so the encyclopedia holds it as a title borne by possibly more than one king, and says so. Phicol, the commander of the army in both accounts, and Ahuzzath, whom the Septuagint names in both, may likewise be titles; that is a supposition, and it is stated as one. Abimelech son of Gideon (JDG 8:31-9:57) is a personal name and stays a person.
source: Essenthos, on the project owner's decision of 2026-09-13 that Abimelech of Gerar, Phicol and Ahuzzath are not established as single persons and are held as titles

titles.name: Abimelech
titles.distinguisher: the name or title of the king of Gerar in the days of Abraham (GEN 20-21) and of Isaac (GEN 26), and of the Philistine king of the title of PSA 34; not certainly one man
titles.notes: The text calls the king of Gerar Abimelech when Abraham sojourns there (GEN 20:1-18) and makes a covenant with him at Beersheba (GEN 21:22-32), and again when Isaac sojourns there after Abraham's death (GEN 26:1-31). The title of Psalm 34 gives the name to the king before whom David feigned madness, whom 1 Samuel 21:10-15 calls Achish king of Gath. Read as one man, he would reach from Abraham to David, which the text nowhere asks for. The likelier reading is that Abimelech, 'my father is king', was a title of the Philistine kings as Pharaoh was of Egypt's, and Jewish tradition reads it so (Rashi). It may therefore be a title borne by more than one king, and the text does not decide whether the Abimelech of Abraham and the Abimelech of Isaac are one man or two. It is not the Abimelech son of Gideon (JDG 8:31-9:57), whose own name it was. In 1 Chronicles 18:16 the Masoretic text also reads Abimelech, for the priest the parallel 2 Samuel 8:17 calls Ahimelech son of Abiathar; that verse means him.
titles.why: The owner ruled that Abimelech of Gerar is not established as one man who dealt with Abraham, with Isaac and, in the title of Psalm 34, with David: it is likely a title of the Philistine kings, as Pharaoh is of Egypt's, and at the least not certainly one person.

replaces.why: A second person record for the Abimelech of Genesis 26, written because a reading judged Isaac's king 'likely a successor bearing the same name'. Held as a title, the name needs no second man to be true of both accounts, and that reading is kept among the alternatives instead.

alternatives.describes: one king of Gerar whose own name was Abimelech, who dealt with Abraham (GEN 20-21) and again with Isaac (GEN 26)
alternatives.reason: Both accounts name him alike, Abimelech king of Gerar with Phicol the commander of his army, and neither says a new king has come. Against it, Isaac's dealings with him fall after Abraham's death (GEN 26:18), most of a lifetime after Abraham's, and the same two names recurring is as well explained by titles as by one very long reign.

alternatives.describes: two kings of Gerar, Abraham's and Isaac's, who both bore Abimelech as a personal name
alternatives.reason: A king named after his father would give the text as it stands, the Abimelech of Genesis 26 another man than the Abimelech of Genesis 20-21. Nothing in the text tells a name repeated in a line of kings from a title.

The title of Psalm 34 says David changed his behaviour before Abimelech, and 1 Samuel 21:10-15 tells the same flight before Achish king of Gath. If Abimelech is a title of the Philistine kings, the king of the psalm is Achish bearing it; if it is a name, the psalm's title and the history name the king differently.
alternatives.back: The title of Psalm 34 says David changed his behaviour before Abimelech, where 1 Samuel 21:10-15 tells the same flight before him. If Abimelech is a title of the Philistine kings, he bore it there; if it is a name, the psalm's title and the history name the king differently.

titles.name: Phicol
titles.distinguisher: named as the commander of the army of Abimelech of Gerar under Abraham (GEN 21:22, 32) and under Isaac (GEN 26:26); possibly a title rather than one man's name
titles.notes: Phicol comes with Abimelech to Abraham at Beersheba (GEN 21:22, 32) and again, after Abraham's death, with Abimelech to Isaac (GEN 26:26), both times as the commander of his army. One commander serving across both accounts is as hard to hold as one king, and the same pair of names recurring suggests that Phicol, like Abimelech, may be a title, that of the commander of the army of Gerar, rather than one man's name. That is a supposition the text does not state.
titles.why: The owner ruled that Phicol, the commander of Abimelech's army in the accounts of both Abraham and Isaac, should not be set up as one separate person: he may be a title, as Abimelech may be. The ruling states it as a supposition.

alternatives.describes: one man named Phicol, who commanded the army of Gerar under Abraham's Abimelech and again under Isaac's (GEN 21:22; 26:26)
alternatives.reason: The text gives the same name and the same office in both accounts and does not say they are two men; if Abimelech was one long-reigning king, one commander serving him throughout is possible.

titles.name: Ahuzzath
titles.distinguisher: named as the friend who came with Abimelech to Isaac (GEN 26:26), and in the Septuagint also beside Abimelech in Abraham's day (GEN 21:22, 32); possibly a title rather than one man's name
titles.notes: The Hebrew names Ahuzzath once, as one of Abimelech's friends, when he and Phicol come to Isaac (GEN 26:26). The Septuagint names him in the account of Abraham as well: Ochozath his friend, ὁ νυμφαγωγὸς αὐτοῦ, stands beside Abimelech and Phicol at GEN 21:22 and 21:32, where the Masoretic text has no Ahuzzath. Named in both generations as the king's companion, he may, like Abimelech and Phicol, be a title, that of the king's friend or counsellor, rather than one man's name. That is a supposition the text does not state.
titles.why: The owner ruled that Ahuzzath should not be set up as one separate person: like Phicol he may be a title, and the Septuagint names him in Abraham's day as well as in Isaac's. The ruling states it as a supposition.

alternatives.describes: one man named Ahuzzath, a friend of the king of Gerar in Isaac's day (GEN 26:26)
alternatives.reason: The Hebrew names him only once, and as one man. His name in the Septuagint's account of Abraham may be that translation bringing the two covenants at Beersheba into line with each other rather than a witness that the name was an office.

titles.name: Pharaoh
titles.distinguisher: the title of the kings of Egypt, which the text uses for eight kings it does not name and for Necho, whom it does
titles.notes: Pharaoh, Hebrew par'oh, is the Egyptian per-aa, 'great house', the palace and then the king who held it; the text uses it as the Egyptian court did, as the way to speak of the reigning king. The king who took Sarai (GEN 12), Joseph's king (GEN 37-50), the king of the oppression (EXO 1-2), the king of the Exodus (EXO 3-15), Solomon's father-in-law (1KI 3:1), the father of Bithiah (1CH 4:18), the king of Isaiah's oracle (ISA 19:11) and the king of Jeremiah's day (JER 25:19) are each called Pharaoh and none of them by a name; each is a man of his own, and the title is what they have in common. Twice the text gives the title and the name together: Pharaoh-nechoh (2KI 23:29) and Pharaoh-hophra (JER 44:30). Shishak and So are called king of Egypt and never Pharaoh.
titles.why: The owner ruled that Pharaoh is held as a title and that every other title the text gives is collected beside it, joined to a bearer only where a verse names the person and the title together.
titles.source: Essenthos, on the project owner's decision of 2026-09-19 that Pharaoh is a title and that the titles the text gives are collected as titles, each joined to the people a verse gives it to

titles.name: Caesar
titles.distinguisher: the title of the Roman emperors, from the family name of Julius Caesar
titles.notes: Caesar was the family name of Julius Caesar, taken by Augustus as his heir and borne after him by every emperor, until it was the title of the office. The Gospels and Acts use it both with a name, Caesar Augustus (LUK 2:1), Tiberius Caesar (LUK 3:1) and Claudius Caesar (ACT 11:28, as the King James and the Textus Receptus read; the critical text has Claudius alone), and alone for whoever reigned: the Caesar to whom tribute is given (MAT 22:17-21) is Tiberius, and the Caesar to whom Paul appeals (ACT 25:8-12) is Nero, whom the text never names.

titles.name: High priest
titles.distinguisher: the chief of the priests, the one who alone entered the most holy place on the Day of Atonement
titles.notes: The Law speaks of the high priest as an office, 'the priest that is great among his brethren' (LEV 21:10), and names him as such only rarely before the exile: Hilkiah under Josiah (2KI 22:4), and after it Joshua son of Josedech (HAG 1:1) and Eliashib (NEH 3:1). In the New Testament the Greek archiereus is both the high priest and, in the plural, the chief priests as a body; the men it names singly are Caiaphas (MAT 26:3), Annas (ACT 4:6), Ananias (ACT 23:2) and, in the Lord's own words, Abiathar (MRK 2:26). Aaron, Eleazar, Eli, Zadok and Jehoiada held the office by every account, but the text calls them the priest rather than the high priest by name.

titles.name: Tetrarch
titles.distinguisher: a Roman client ruler of a part of a kingdom, below a king
titles.notes: Literally the ruler of a fourth part, and by the first century any client ruler of a portion of a divided kingdom, below the rank of king. Herod the Great's realm was divided among his sons, and Luke dates the Baptist's ministry by three tetrarchs: Herod over Galilee, his brother Philip over Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias over Abilene (LUK 3:1). Matthew and Mark also call Herod Antipas king (MAT 14:9; MRK 6:14), which is the courtesy of the people rather than his rank.

titles.name: Anointed (Messiah, Christ)
titles.distinguisher: the title of one anointed to an office, Hebrew mashiach and Greek Christos: given to the anointed priest, to Saul, to David, to Cyrus and to Jesus
titles.notes: Mashiach, 'anointed', is said of one on whom oil was poured to set him apart for an office. Leviticus says it of the priest, 'the priest that is anointed' (LEV 4:3, 4:5, 4:16; 6:22). From Samuel on it is the king, 'the LORD's anointed': Saul in the mouth of David, who would not stretch forth his hand against him (1SA 24:6, 24:10; 26:9, 26:11, 26:16, 26:23; 2SA 1:14, 1:16), and David himself (2SA 19:21; 22:51; 23:1; PSA 18:50). Once it is a foreign king, Cyrus of Persia (ISA 45:1). In the Psalms and the Prophets it often stands with no name beside it (PSA 2:2; DAN 9:25-26). The Septuagint renders it Christos, and the New Testament takes that word up; John gives the Hebrew word once as Messias and translates it, 'which is, being interpreted, the Christ' (JHN 1:41). The Gospels record the question being asked of John the Baptist and of Jesus (LUK 3:15; JHN 1:20; 10:24; MAT 26:63) and answer that Jesus is the Christ (MAT 16:16; JHN 20:31); in the letters Christ stands beside his name and in place of it.
titles.why: The owner ruled that the Anointed, mashiach in Hebrew and Christos and Messias in Greek, is held as a title, as Pharaoh is: joined to the bearers a verse gives it to, and named at every word the text writes it with.

titles.name: Giant
titles.distinguisher: a man of great stature, as the text calls the Nephilim, the Rephaim and the Anakim, and those born to the giant in Gath (GEN 6:4; DEU 2:11; 2SA 21:22)
titles.notes: Three Hebrew words are rendered giants. Nephilim: 'there were giants in the earth in those days' (GEN 6:4), and the spies saw 'the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants' (NUM 13:33). Rephaim, a people of the land before Israel, 'accounted giants, as the Anakims', whom the Moabites call Emims (DEU 2:10-11) and the Ammonites Zamzummims (DEU 2:20); of their remnant was Og king of Bashan, whose bedstead of iron was nine cubits long (DEU 3:11). And ha-rapha, 'the giant' in Gath, to whom were born Ishbi-benob, Saph, Goliath the Gittite and a man of great stature with six fingers on every hand and six toes on every foot, who fell by the hand of David and of his servants (2SA 21:16-22); Chronicles names Lahmi the brother of Goliath among them (1CH 20:5-8). Goliath's height was six cubits and a span (1SA 17:4).
titles.why: The owner ruled that every giant's line says giant, as an angel's says angel: the text's own word for them, held as the title the archangel is, joined to each giant at the verse that calls him or his people so.

rulings.why: The title of the psalm: David changed his behaviour before Abimelech, the Philistine king 1 Samuel 21:10-15 calls Achish king of Gath. It is the name or title the entry holds, and whether it is Achish's title or a second name for him is what the entry leaves open.

The Septuagint reads Abimelech, and Ochozath his friend, and Phicol the commander of his army, where the Masoretic text has Abimelech and Phicol alone; Codex Vaticanus and Brenton's text both name him here. Ochozath is the Greek of Ahuzzath in GEN 26:26.
Phicol the commander of Abimelech's army, as the Masoretic text names him in this verse.
As in GEN 21:22, the Septuagint has Abimelech rise with Ochozath his friend and Phicol, where the Masoretic text has no Ahuzzath.
Phicol the commander of Abimelech's army, as the Masoretic text names him in this verse.
Ochozath his friend, the Ahuzzath of the Masoretic text in this verse.
